posts.character: Cars and driving culture (the glove box road map)
posts.quote: THE ROAD MAP CAME OUT OF THE GLOVE BOX ONCE A YEAR, AND NOBODY EVER FOLDED IT BACK THE RIGHT WAY.
posts.caption: The road map lived in the glove box all year, under the registration and a flashlight that never worked. Once a summer it came out, usually in the driveway with the whole family watching. Dad spread it across the hood and traced a route with one finger, and Mom looked at it from the other side and said it was upside down. It wasn't, but it never helped to say so. When they finally agreed on the route, the map went back in the glove box folded in some brand new way that none of its creases had ever planned for. By the next summer it was a different shape again, and the whole thing started over.
posts.first: My father had one rule about the map: whoever opened it had to be the one to fold it. That rule lasted until about the second creek. I still have one of those maps in a drawer, and I still can't get it back the way it came.

posts.quote: THE CALENDAR FROM THE BANK HUNG BY THE KITCHEN DOOR, AND EVERY BIRTHDAY AND DENTIST VISIT WAS WRITTEN ON IT IN PENCIL.
posts.caption: Every kitchen had a calendar from the bank or the hardware store, hung from a single nail beside the door. It had a picture of a red barn or a covered bridge at the top and a grid of squares underneath. Nobody wrote on it in pen, because pencil could be changed. Birthdays went in first, then the dentist, the church supper, and the day the furnace man was coming. A pencil hung beside it on a piece of string, so there was never an excuse. By the end of the month the whole page was a record of where the family had been and where it was supposed to be. When the new one came after Christmas, the old one got saved for the picture.
posts.first: My grandmother kept her old calendars in a drawer by the stove, one for every year. After she was gone we found them, and you could read the whole decade in them, right down to what she paid the paperboy. I took the 1966 one.
